get.description:
The authoring audit trail: who changed which rule/variable/scorecard/policy, when.

This route did not exist. Events were written -- and after the entity-CRUD wiring, written
for every authoring entity -- but nothing read them back over HTTP, so the compliance
artifact this product exists to produce could only be reached by opening the database. An
auditor asking "show me every change to this rule" had no answer.

limit/offset use the Annotated form so the PYTHON default is a real int. Written as
`limit: int = Query(default=200, ...)` the default value is a `Query` object, which FastAPI
unwraps but a direct call does not -- so any test or internal caller invoking the handler as
a plain function got a `Query` where an int was promised and failed inside SQLAlchemy with
`'<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'Query'`. Same validation, no trap.

limit/offset are BOUNDED HERE, not in storage. `list_audit_events` deliberately applies them
raw -- its internal callers pass limit=None to mean "every matching event" -- so this route is
the only place that can reject a nonsense page. Untyped, `?limit=-1` reached Postgres as
`LIMIT -1` and answered 500 (`InvalidRowCountInLimitClause`) on the one endpoint an auditor's
tooling drives; on SQLite the same request was quieter and worse, because `LIMIT -1` means NO
limit there and the unbounded fetch this signature exists to prevent came back silently.

Tenant is passed explicitly rather than relying on the storage layer's fallback chain
(`tenant_id or contextvar or default_tenant_id`). On an authenticated request the contextvar
is set by the middleware and resolves correctly either way -- but the last link in that
chain is the FIRST tenant, and an audit read reaching it would serve one tenant's change
history to another. Cheap to not depend on.

Liveness. Deliberately static: no database, no Redis, no I/O of any kind.

This used to call _dependency_status() and answer 503 whenever Postgres was unreachable,
and the Helm chart points its LIVENESS probe here. The two together mean a 30-second DB
failover — a survivable event — fails liveness on every replica at once and kubelet
restarts the entire API fleet, turning a brief dependency blip into a full outage with a
cold-start thundering herd on the database that just came back.

It was also a sync `def`, so FastAPI ran it on the same bounded threadpool as /decide: a
saturated sandbox pool could time the probe out and trigger the same mass restart with
every dependency perfectly healthy. `async def` keeps it on the event loop, where nothing
a request handler does can starve it.

Liveness answers one question — is this process still able to serve? — and only a restart
fixes a "no". Whether the dependencies are reachable is READINESS, and it stays on /ready,
where a "no" takes the pod out of the load-balancer rotation and puts it back by itself.

The machine-readable API contract, behind the ordinary API-key check.

THE GAP THIS CLOSES. `/openapi.json`, `/docs` and `/redoc` are all disabled when
RULEMIND_ENV is production (see `_docs_enabled` -- correctly, they were served
unauthenticated and handed the complete endpoint map to anyone who asked), and the Helm
chart sets exactly that. So **a Helm install published no API contract at all**, and the
human fallback is `API.md`, which documented 17 of 278 endpoints and got 13 of the 17
wrong -- naming `/api/v1/api-keys` (really `/api/v1/access/keys`), `/api/v1/approvals`
(really `/api/v1/reviews`), `POST /api/v1/rules/validate` (does not exist) and
`/api/v1/dashboard/summary` (does not exist). An integration team following the shipped
documentation gets 404s.

Removing the spec was the right fix for the wrong reason: the problem was that it was
PUBLIC, not that it existed. This path is not in `middleware.EXEMPT_PATHS`, so it requires
a valid API key like every other `/api/v1/` route -- the customer's own integration team
can generate a typed client, and an unauthenticated scanner still gets nothing.

Served regardless of RULEMIND_ENV, deliberately: production is exactly where a self-hosted
customer needs it, and `RULEMIND_ENABLE_DOCS` stays the separate switch for the PUBLIC
Swagger UI.

What it types (plan 5.1): the responses an integration depends on -- decide and batch
decide, decision records, reason codes, replay, OAuth2 tokens, the SDK endpoints, data
subjects and residency, executions, liveness and readiness -- plus the error envelope on
every operation and the credentials each one needs. The rest of the authoring surface still
documents its responses as open objects; `app/api_models.py` is where a type is added.

storage drops the None ones, so the request already reads as a patch -- but `update_settings`

post.description:
Diagnostics for the editor, WITHOUT running the code (P13).

The editor needs to say "line 4: unexpected indent" or "line 7: Import not allowed: os"
before the author clicks Test. Doing that in the browser would mean a Python parser in
JavaScript and a second copy of the sandbox policy -- two implementations that would drift
from the ones that actually decide whether the code runs, and a linter that disagrees with
the runtime is worse than no linter, because the author learns to ignore it.

So this reuses `sandbox.validate_source`: the exact function the sandbox calls before
executing anything. A diagnostic here is therefore not an approximation of the rule, it IS
the rule.

It does not EXECUTE. `test-draft` above already does that, in a real sandbox with a timeout
and a memory cap; this is the cheap check that runs while someone is typing, so it must not
spawn a process or touch a connector.

get.description:
Liveness. Deliberately static: no database, no Redis, no I/O of any kind.

This used to call _dependency_status() and answer 503 whenever Postgres was unreachable,
and the Helm chart points its LIVENESS probe here. The two together mean a 30-second DB
failover — a survivable event — fails liveness on every replica at once and kubelet
restarts the entire API fleet, turning a brief dependency blip into a full outage with a
cold-start thundering herd on the database that just came back.

It was also a sync `def`, so FastAPI ran it on the same bounded threadpool as /decide: a
saturated sandbox pool could time the probe out and trigger the same mass restart with
every dependency perfectly healthy. `async def` keeps it on the event loop, where nothing
a request handler does can starve it.

Liveness answers one question — is this process still able to serve? — and only a restart
fixes a "no". Whether the dependencies are reachable is READINESS, and it stays on /ready,
where a "no" takes the pod out of the load-balancer rotation and puts it back by itself.

get.description:
Readiness — the ONLY probe that touches the dependencies.

A readinessProbe only looks at the status code, so returning 200 with {"ready": false}
— as this used to — meant the gate never fired. Failing here is safe in a way failing
/health is not: the pod leaves the service endpoints and rejoins on its own the moment
the dependency recovers, with no restart and no lost warm state.

Serve a single policy as a self-contained, cacheable **decision block**.

Unlike the full tenant bundle, a block carries exactly one production policy plus only the
rules / scorecards / decision tables it references (and the compiled variables). A client
fetches one block, caches it by its ETag (the block checksum), and evaluates that policy
on-device with the same SDK evaluators. Supports conditional GET (If-None-Match → 304) and
optional per-client encryption when an `X-Client-Public-Key` header is supplied.

Ingest a batch of on-device decisions from a device's local outbox.

Idempotent and retry-safe: a decision whose client-stable `id` already exists (or
repeats within the batch) is acknowledged but NOT duplicated — so a device can retry
with exponential backoff without ever double-counting. The response's `acked` list is
exactly the ids the device may now clear locally. Requires the `decide` capability.
